deep.reconstruction:
There are no derivations or computations on this page. It is a sheet of programmatic and philosophical notes on foundations, with cross-references to Hilbert's own notebooks. Item by item:

(1) 'I, II, III sind die schwarzen Hefte': a key saying that the Roman numerals I, II, III refer to his black notebooks. 'S. H.' below means Schwarzes Heft.

(2) 'Frage B, ob Frage A durch endl. Anzahl von Operationen entscheidbar [ist]', with reference 'S.H. I S. 50'. This is a meta-question. Given a mathematical question A, question B asks whether A can be decided by a finite number of operations. In modern terms it is the question of decidability or effective solvability, a second-order question about a problem rather than the problem itself. It is the germ of what became the Entscheidungsproblem and the metamathematical programme. It also echoes the 'finite number of operations' wording of the 1900 Paris problems (e.g. the 10th problem).

(3) 'Ferner [?] Endlichkeitsbeweise ohne und mit oberer Grenze': finiteness proofs without and with an upper bound. This is the distinction between pure existence finiteness proofs and effective ones that supply a bound. Hilbert's 1890 basis theorem is the famous example of the first kind; Gordan objected to it. Bounds for ideal-theoretic and invariant-theoretic finiteness came later, e.g. Grete Hermann 1926.

(4) 'Die 10^(10^10)-te Dez[imale] von π finden', with 'z.B. [illegible reference] II S. 0–1'. This is the standard example of a question that is decidable in principle by a finite computation but practically out of reach. It contrasts finite decidability with practical feasibility. Brouwer and Weyl later used digit patterns in the expansion of π as examples of undecided propositions.

(5) 'Existenz = Widerspruchsfreiheit': existence equals consistency. This is Hilbert's well-known dictum from his 1899 correspondence with Frege and the 1900 Paris address, 2nd problem.

(6) Methodological aphorism: detail work receives its true (perhaps 'highest') consecration only when the view is directed to generality and to knowledge of the foundations.

(7) The researcher must be freed from the worry, the unconscious fear (expressed as excessive modesty and discouragement), that it might be impossible for the human mind ever to penetrate somewhere to full knowledge. This is the anti-'Ignorabimus' theme of the 1900 address ('in der Mathematik gibt es kein Ignorabimus') and of the 1930 Königsberg talk ('Wir müssen wissen, wir werden wissen').

(8) 'Alles was Gegenstand des Denkens ist, ist Gegenstand der Math[ematik]. Diese ...' (the rest is cut off or illegible). Compare 'Axiomatisches Denken' (1917/18): everything that can be an object of scientific thought falls under the axiomatic method and thereby mediately under mathematics.

The content fits Hilbert's foundational notes. The meta-question about decidability fits the 1900–1920s period, where it has no direct companion; the cross-referencing to the black notebooks fits a later compilation of themes.

The only mildly interesting detail is the explicit labelling of decidability as a separate 'Frage B' about 'Frage A', cross-referenced to his black notebook. Even that is in line with known material.
